title: Let the dead bury their dead (Matthew 8:14–22)
word: Let the dead bury their dead
hookLine: a hard saying: following doesn't wait for a convenient time
tomorrow: what kind of person does a storm obey?
last: MANY SHALL COME FROM EAST AND WEST.

cards: Calendars fill up with afters: after exams, after the move, after things settle down. Capernaum, evening.
Jesus has just healed Peter's mother-in-law: "He touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them." A crowd has come with their sick, and he heals them.
Now he gives the word to cross the lake, and two men step up to follow. One of them has a request that couldn't sound more reasonable. It's about a funeral.

teach.b: The first is a scribe, a teacher of the law, all promise: "Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest." Jesus doesn't turn him away.
He tells him the cost: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head."
Then a disciple: "Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father." It sounds completely fair. The commandments say, "Honour thy father and thy mother."
And Jesus answers: "Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead." Matthew doesn't explain it, and readers differ. Some think the father hadn't died yet, and the man meant someday, once he's gone.
Some hear the first dead as people dead to God's call, burying their own. Some hear a deliberate shock, said to wake him.
Notice the word first in the man's request, and the two words Jesus begins with: follow me. Not when things settle. Now.
It's said to one man at one moment; Matthew doesn't make it a rule about funerals, or about grief.
But it sits right beside the scribe who promised too much too fast, and both get the same answer: the real cost, in the present tense.

how: Some Christians treat the call to follow me as daily and present, and in some traditions people answer it with a fresh start each morning rather than waiting for a better time.

games.q: what does “let the dead bury their dead” mean?
o: a hard call to follow now, not later
a rule that the dead must bury themselves
a curse spoken over an unfaithful town

games.q: a friend says she'll start volunteering at the animal shelter once senior year calms down. she's said it since sophomore year. what fits today's story?
o: start with one shift this month, not someday.
wait for a calmer year; timing has to be right.
sign up for every shift at once to make up for it.
games.why: to the man who asked to go first, Jesus said follow me. in Matthew the call comes in the present tense, sized to one real step.

practice: Pick up your phone and find the message you keep meaning to send: the thank-you, the check-in, the apology sitting in versions. Send it now, or, if now truly isn't right, set it to go at the first moment it can.
Then put the phone face down and rest.

wordCard.voice: Let the dead bury their dead. A hard saying with more than one reading, and one plain center: follow me.

orig.note: Greek: follow me. Jesus' first words to the man in Matthew 8:22.

carryVoice: Keep this one: follow now, not after things settle, and not some better day. Sleep well.
